before: We study why Gemma 4 31B, as a coding agent with thinking off, sends the same tool call again and again until its budget runs out. On 109 tasks in the harness of Kaggle's Gemma 4 Developer Agent competition, at least half the calls are repeats or malformed in a quarter of task runs, and these runs resolve 20% of the time, against 37%. Using one-step replays at fixed histories and whole-task runs under three levers, we find that: (1) the chance of one more identical call rises from 78% after two calls to 99% after ten even when a proxy holds the request fixed, so most of the rise is selection of states where the model is already near certain of the call, and identical copies in context add to it; (2) loops can be broken but not removed: where the model, free to think, chose not to, a forced thought lets the next call escape 58% of the time, against 11%; and (3) no lever measurably changes resolution.
after: We study why Gemma 4 31B, as a coding agent with thinking off, sends the same tool call again and again until its budget runs out. On 109 tasks in the harness of Kaggle's Gemma 4 Developer Agent competition, at least half the calls are repeats or malformed in a quarter of task runs, and these runs resolve 20% of the time, against 37%. Using one-step replays at fixed histories and whole-task runs under three levers, we obtain three findings. (1) The chance of one more identical call rises from 78% after two calls to 99% after ten even with a fixed request, showing that accumulating copies is unnecessary for increasing persistence. Fixed-history edits independently show that identical copies reinforce immediate repetition. (2) One-step escapes can be induced: where the model, free to think, chose not to, a forced thought lets the next call escape 58% of the time, against 11%. (3) None of the three whole-task interventions produced a detectable improvement in resolution under the tested budget.

before: (1) Lock-in is mostly selection. With a proxy that holds the request fixed, the chance of one more identical call still rises from 78% to 99%, and identical copies add to it. Gemma 4 12B, without the proxy, locks in at the same rates (§4).
after: (1) Persistence rises even with a fixed request. Continuation increases from 78% to 99% under the proxy, consistent with selection of persistent states; fixed-history edits separately establish reinforcement by identical copies. The two model sizes show similar continuation curves once copying has begun (§4).

before: (2) Loops end from outside: at T = 0.2 the agent never ended a run of five or more identical calls itself, in 1,342 chances (§5).
after: (2) In the 31B control at T = 0.2, no spontaneous exit occurred in 1,342 observed clean transitions after five or more identical, well-formed calls (§5).

before: (4) No lever that breaks loops measurably changes resolution (§7).
after: (4) The three whole-task interventions alter repetition, but none produces a detectable improvement in resolution under the tested budget (§7).

before: A call is stale if it repeats an earlier one (same tool and arguments) with no successful file edit since, and a copy if that call came just before. A malformed call's arguments do not fit the tool. A loop task run has at least half its calls stale or malformed. After k identical calls, the hazard h(k) is the probability that the next is identical too, counted on clean steps: no budget warning in the last result and no compaction before the call. An escape, one step ahead, is a sampled call that is neither stale nor malformed. Intervals are 95%, from resampling tasks.
after: A call is stale if it repeats an earlier one (same tool and arguments) with no successful file edit since, and a copy if that call came just before. A malformed call's arguments do not fit the tool. A loop task run has at least half its calls stale or malformed. After k identical calls, h(k) is the probability that the next call is identical. Figure 1b uses transitions following well-formed calls on clean steps: no budget warning in the last result and no compaction before the next call. For the proxy at k ≥ 2, the figure additionally requires that the entire current run was collapsed. Paired differences reported for all well-formed steps use a separate population. The conventional exit hazard is 1 − h(k). An escape, one step ahead, is a sampled call that is neither stale nor malformed. Intervals are 95%, from resampling tasks.

before: In the control, a fresh call is followed by an identical one 2.4% of the time. After two identical calls the hazard is 0.68, after three or four 0.96, and from five on the agent continued at every clean step (Fig. 1b). Two mechanisms predict a curve that rises like this. Under reinforcement, each copy in context makes the next one likelier, as repetition does in text generation (Xu et al., 2022). Under selection, runs start where the model is already near certain of the call, and the longer a run lasts, the more it consists of such states.
after: In the control, a fresh call is followed by an identical one 2.4% of the time. After two identical calls the continuation probability is 0.68, after three or four 0.96, and from five on the agent continued at every clean step (Fig. 1b). Two mechanisms predict a curve that rises like this. Reinforcement predicts that added copies increase the chance of another copy at a fixed history. Selection also predicts increasing continuation: under a fixed request, states with higher repeat probabilities are more likely to survive to longer runs. The proxy tests whether the curve can rise without accumulating copies; the fixed-history edits test reinforcement directly.

before: A rising hazard is no evidence of reinforcement by itself. Suppose each states draws the same call again with a fixed probability p, as it does when the request is held fixed. Over the states where runs start, , and since  (Cauchy–Schwarz), h(k) never falls with k, whatever the mix of states. This is the frailty effect of survival analysis, where differences between individuals alone make a population's hazard rise (Vaupel et al., 1979). The proxy separates the two mechanisms: with the request fixed, any rise is selection, and the gap to the control is what the copies add (Fig. 1a).
after: A rising continuation probability alone does not establish reinforcement. Suppose each state s draws the same call again with a fixed probability p, as it does when the request is held fixed. Over the states where runs start, , and since  (Cauchy–Schwarz), h(k) never falls with k, whatever the mix of states. This is analogous to frailty selection in survival analysis (Vaupel et al., 1979): more persistent states become enriched among survivors, so continuation rises and the corresponding exit hazard falls. Under a fixed request and stationary, independent draws within a state, the rise can arise through selection alone. Because the two arms reach different states and retain different survivors, their gap does not identify the fraction of the control curve caused by accumulating copies.

before: With the request fixed, the hazard still rises: 0.78 after two identical calls, 0.87 after three or four, 0.93 after five to nine and 0.99 after ten or more. Most of the curve's height is selection. The copies add nothing measurable at k = 2 (proxy minus control, paired over tasks: +7.6 points, −8.9 to +22.4). From three calls on, they close the escapes that remain: −7.0 points (−13.3 to −0.8) at three or four, and −4.1 (−7.3 to −1.1) at five to nine. Without the copies in view the agent ends 47% of its runs of three or more itself, against 15% (+32 points, +20 to +45), yet about three quarters of its runs of ten or more persist. One step ahead, at 60 fixed histories after a search that found nothing, identical copies raise the probability of the same search from 0.002 with one copy to 0.43 with four. Re-spelled copies of it, with the same results, leave it near 0.03. The copies reinforce on their exact tokens.
after: With the request fixed, the continuation probability still rises: 0.78 after two identical calls, 0.87 after three or four, 0.93 after five to nine and 0.99 after ten or more. High continuation persists without accumulating copies. In a separate analysis of all well-formed steps, paired differences over tasks (proxy minus control) are +7.6 points (−8.9 to +22.4) at k = 2, −7.0 (−13.3 to −0.8) at k = 3–4, and −4.1 (−7.3 to −1.1) at k = 5–9. These estimates include warning and compaction transitions and are not differences between the clean, fully collapsed values in Figure 1b. The between-arm differences are consistent with a contribution from copies, which the fixed-history edits test directly. Among runs of three or more calls that ended before the task, own exits occurred in 43 of 91 proxy runs (47%) and 16 of 107 control runs (15%; difference +32 points, +20 to +45). Runs of ten or more occurred 0.25 times per task under the proxy versus 0.33 under the control, about three quarters as often. This ratio compares incidence across arms, not matched survival of the same runs. One step ahead, at 60 fixed histories after a search that found nothing, identical copies raise the probability of the same search from 0.002 with one copy to 0.43 with four. Re-spelled copies of it, with the same results, leave it near 0.03. The copies reinforce on their exact tokens.

before: Gemma 4 12B starts runs more readily: it copies a fresh call 5.8% of the time, against 2.4% (+3.2 points, +2.2 to +4.2). From k = 2 on its hazard matches the 31B's, and no difference's interval excludes zero. Size moves the onset, not the lock-in. We did not run the proxy at 12B, so selection is measured at 31B only.
after: On clean steps, Gemma 4 12B copies a fresh call 5.8% of the time, versus 2.4% for 31B. A separate all-step comparison gives +3.2 points (+2.2 to +4.2). Once copying begins, the observed continuation curves are similar; the all-step paired intervals include zero, which does not establish equivalence. We did not run the proxy at 12B, so the fixed-request selection test is limited to 31B.

before: At T = 0.2 the agent does not end a long run itself. On clean steps it continued every run of five or more identical calls: 290 of 290 steps at five to nine calls and 1,052 of 1,052 at ten or more. Of the 58 well-formed runs of ten or more, 43 ended after the harness's budget warning (“Only 10 tool call(s) remaining …”), 14 at a context compaction and one with the task. Neither exit helps much: after the warning at most ten calls remain, and after a compaction the agent sends the same call again 30–41% of the time. With the request held fixed, long runs end the same way (31 of 54 at the warning), and Gemma 4 12B ends only 4 of its 119 runs of ten or more itself. Past five calls, only a change from outside ends a run; most often it is the warning, an instruction.
after: In the 31B control at T = 0.2, no spontaneous exit was observed after five or more identical, well-formed calls on clean steps: 290 of 290 transitions continued at k = 5–9 and 1,052 of 1,052 at k ≥ 10. Of the 58 well-formed runs of ten or more, 43 ended after the harness's budget warning (“Only 10 tool call(s) remaining …”), 14 at a context compaction and one with the task. Neither exit helps much: after the warning at most ten calls remain, and after a compaction the agent sends the same call again 30–41% of the time. With the request held fixed, long runs end the same way (31 of 54 at the warning), and Gemma 4 12B ends only 4 of its 119 runs of ten or more itself. These observed long control runs ended following a budget warning, at compaction, or with task termination; this descriptive classification does not by itself identify the causal effect of either intervention. Malformed runs and the 12B control can end spontaneously.

before: Table 1. Whole-task levers against the control, Gemma 4 31B on 109 tasks unless noted. Differences are lever minus control in percentage points, paired over tasks, with 95% intervals from 2,000 task resamples. The 12B row shows the size of change the design detects.
after: Table 1. Whole-task levers against the control, Gemma 4 31B on 109 tasks unless noted. Differences are lever minus control, paired over tasks, with 95% intervals from 2,000 task resamples. Resolution and share differences are in percentage points; run-length and frequency differences use calls and runs per task, respectively. The 12B comparison provides an observed large contrast, rather than a formal estimate of the minimum detectable effect.

before: None of them measurably changes resolution, and breaking a loop does not recover the task. T = 1 un-looped 46 of the control's 54 loop task runs: the control solved 10 of those tasks and T = 1 solved 9, spending the freed budget on new calls and source edits. In 23 of 24 such tasks in the first pass, the control's first stale call came before its first source edit. In the early run of §1, only 6 of the 23 failures with many repeats were solved by any of nine other agent runs, about 2 of 70 tasks. The design detects a change the size of the 12B's (−22.0 points) but not one of one or two tasks, since a single run varies by about ±2.2 tasks. An inconclusive difference is not equivalence.
after: None of the three interventions produced a detectable improvement in resolution under the tested budget. T = 1 un-looped 46 of the control's 54 loop task runs: the control solved 10 of those tasks and T = 1 solved 9, spending the freed budget on new calls and source edits. In 23 of 24 such tasks in the first pass, the control's first stale call came before its first source edit. In the early run of §1, only 6 of the 23 failures with many repeats were solved by any of nine other agent runs, about 2 of 70 tasks. The resolution intervals retain uncertainty about small and moderate benefits; the two-pass design does not establish equivalence. The large 12B contrast is readily observed, while the effects of improving a small number of task runs remain uncertain. The cross-run rescue count describes the tested runs and does not bound what a new intervention could recover.

before: Repetition in text. Generators repeat themselves more with each repetition in context (Holtzman et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022), and reasoning models loop at low temperature, where raising it is “a stopgap” (Pipis et al., 2026). Our tool-call loops show the same rising curve, but holding the request fixed shows that most of it is selection, not self-reinforcement.
after: Repetition in text. Generators repeat themselves more with each repetition in context (Holtzman et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022), and reasoning models loop at low temperature, where raising it is “a stopgap” (Pipis et al., 2026). Our tool-call loops show a similar rising curve, and holding the request fixed demonstrates that such a curve can arise without accumulating copies; fixed-history edits separately show reinforcement by identical copies.

before: Repeats as symptoms. In SWE-smith, warnings, resampling and temperature bumps cut repeats while resolution fell, and the authors read repeats as “symptoms of the model's difficulty” (Yang et al., 2025). Our three levers test that reading, and none raises resolution. Fork-and-Flush escapes idea basins when fresh-context branches are scored and the best is kept (Cai et al., 2026); a coding agent has no such score during a run, and removing the copies does not help it solve more.
after: Repeats as symptoms. In SWE-smith, warnings, resampling and temperature bumps cut repeats while resolution fell, and the authors read repeats as “symptoms of the model's difficulty” (Yang et al., 2025). Our three whole-task interventions provide further evidence that reducing repetition alone need not improve resolution, although their confidence intervals do not exclude useful benefits. Fork-and-Flush escapes idea basins when fresh-context branches are scored and the best is kept (Cai et al., 2026); a coding agent has no such score during a run, and removing the copies produced no detectable increase in resolution in our experiment.

before: The evidence comes from two sizes of one model family (int4), with thinking off, in one harness, on 109 tasks from four repositories. The mechanisms and the levers were measured at 31B only; the 12B tests the descriptive claims. Two passes cannot detect a change of one or two tasks. The forced thought was tested one step ahead, never over whole tasks, and an escape one step ahead need not be progress. The probabilities we report are re-draws of the same call, not calibrated confidence, and nothing here looks inside the model. The empty-thought template and the proxy test mechanisms, not entries: a competition submission can change neither the chat template nor the requests.
after: The evidence comes from two sizes of one model family (int4), with thinking off, in one harness, on 109 tasks from four repositories. The mechanisms and the levers were measured at 31B only; the 12B tests the descriptive claims. With two passes, the resolution estimates remain too uncertain to establish equivalence or exclude benefits affecting only a small number of tasks. The forced thought was tested one step ahead, never over whole tasks, and an escape one step ahead need not be progress. The probabilities we report are re-draws of the same call, not calibrated confidence, and nothing here looks inside the model. The empty-thought template and the proxy test mechanisms, not entries: a competition submission can change neither the chat template nor the requests.

before: Three things follow for agent builders. Lock-in is near complete by the third identical call, earlier than common detectors act. Raising the temperature, breaking the pattern or removing the copies ends loops without recovering the task; our reading is that the loop marks a state the model is already sure of rather than causing the failure. A lever worth testing next acts where the model chose not to think, or brings the agent information it lacks. Breaking a loop frees budget, but it does not recover the task.
after: Three things follow for agent builders. Lock-in is near complete by the third identical call, earlier than common detectors act. Raising the temperature, breaking the pattern, and removing copies altered repetition without producing a detectable resolution improvement. The results are consistent with loops marking difficult states, while leaving open a causal contribution of repetition to failure. A lever worth testing next acts where the model chose not to think, or brings the agent information it lacks. Breaking a loop can free budget, but these interventions did not demonstrate improved task recovery under the tested conditions.
